articles.title: Is this the first glimpse of dark matter? Data point excites physicists
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 01 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01985-9An experiment spots an energy flash similar to that of the long-sought weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP.
articles.content:
An image captured with the Hubble Space Telescope shows the distribution of dark matter in the center of the giant galaxy cluster.Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/IAA, University of Basque Country/JHU

It is a single data point, but enough to send a shiver down physicists’ spines. Some time in 2023 or 2024, a detector containing 10 tonnes of ultra-pure liquid xenon registered an unusual energetic flash. It was the type of signal that could be caused by a collision between an atom’s nucleus and a massive dark-matter particle as it passes through our Galaxy.

If the finding can be backed up with more data, it could mean that dark matter — the invisible stuff that is thought to keep galaxies from flying apart — has finally been discovered. And it would show that dark matter consists of particles much more massive than protons, namely the ‘weakly interacting massive particles’ (WIMPs) that have been theorized but remained undetected despite decades of searching.

Researchers working with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota, announced the result on 1 September at the TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Tendo, Japan, and describe it in a preprint posted on the experiment’s website1.

Previous experiments have seen hopeful signs of dark matter that turned out to be spurious, researchers warn. But LZ’s single outlier event “is intriguing, and will undoubtedly excite the field”, says Jianglai Liu, a physicist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China.

A high-energy event

Crunch time for pet theory on dark matter

For decades, theoreticians have posited that the prime component of dark matter is a WIMP. But attempts to detect the dark matter while it traverses Earth, or to create it by smashing atoms at facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) near Geneva, Switzerland, have come up empty. Many researchers have turned their attention to other possible candidates, such as very light particles.

LZ, which started up in late 2021, is a scaled-up version of earlier experiments that aimed at the ‘direct detection’ of dark matter using xenon. In the study, Samuel Eriksen, the LZ researcher who presented the result at the Tendo conference, and his collaborators analysed 220 days of observational data taken from March 2023 to April 2024.

They focused on rare flashes that occur when a high-energy particle collides with a xenon nucleus, making it recoil at a high speed. “Typically, these searches focus on low energies, meaning less than 50 kiloelectronvolts of energy being deposited” on the xenon nucleus, says Eriksen, a particle physicist at the University of Bristol, UK. “In this analysis, we extended that up to 270 keV.”

The LZ central detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota.Credit: Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory

Both LZ and two competing series of experiments — XENON at Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratories and PandaX at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory in Sichuan — had conducted searches in this energy range before, says Eriksen. But they could do so only on smaller sets of data from earlier, smaller version of their detectors, and had found nothing beyond the expected background of spurious events, such as high-energy neutrons produced by background radiation.

To avoid its own biases, the LZ collaboration ‘salts’ its data during each analysis with numerous randomly produced events that mimic what dark-matter events would look like, says Richard Gaitskell, a physicist at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, and LZ spokesperson. Only when the researchers are done with a batch of data do they ‘unsalt’ it to see whether any remaining dark-matter signals were genuine.

“After we unsalted, there was a single event that was left,” says Gaitskell. “Obviously, that was very exciting.”

The ‘excess’ event was a recoil that deposited 248 keV of energy in the detector. The LZ researchers estimate that a dark-matter particle producing this recoil would have to weigh the equivalent of at least 200 gigaelectronvolts (GeV), and probably around 1,000 GeV (1 GeV corresponds roughly to the mass of a proton).

“What we observe is just one high-energy event,” says Eriksen. “We’re not claiming this is dark matter at all.”

articles.reasoning: The article reports a potentially groundbreaking scientific discovery: the first possible direct detection of dark matter particles, which would be a major breakthrough in astrophysics and cosmology with broad implications for understanding the universe. The finding comes from a large-scale, well-documented experiment with significant context and detail, and while preliminary, it inspires hope and curiosity about solving a fundamental cosmic mystery.
articles.personality_title: Scientists spot a possible sign of dark matter for the first time
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dark matter is a mysterious substance that makes up much of the universe but cannot be seen. Scientists believe it holds galaxies together, but no one has ever directly detected its particles.

**What happened** – Between 2023 and 2024, an experiment called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) in South Dakota recorded a rare energy flash in a tank filled with 10 tonnes of liquid xenon. This flash might have been caused by a dark matter particle hitting a xenon atom. The LZ team shared this finding on September 1, 2026, after studying 220 days of data.

**Impact** – This single event is important because it matches what scientists expected from a type of dark matter particle called a WIMP (weakly interacting massive particle). If confirmed, it would be the first direct evidence of dark matter particles, a discovery that has eluded researchers for decades despite many attempts.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to gather more data to see if they can detect more similar events. Other experiments around the world will also try to confirm or challenge this result. This process will help determine if the flash was truly caused by dark matter or something else.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, scientists may have caught a glimpse of dark matter particles through a rare energy signal detected deep underground.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques détectent peut-être pour la première fois une trace de matière noire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La matière noire est une substance mystérieuse qui compose une grande partie de l’univers, mais qu’on ne peut pas voir. Les scientifiques pensent qu’elle maintient les galaxies ensemble, mais aucun n’a jamais détecté directement ses particules.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Entre 2023 et 2024, une expérience appelée LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dans le Dakota du Sud a enregistré un rare éclair d’énergie dans un réservoir contenant 10 tonnes de xénon liquide. Cet éclair pourrait avoir été causé par une particule de matière noire frappant un atome de xénon. L’équipe LZ a partagé cette découverte le 1er septembre 2026, après avoir étudié 220 jours de données.

**Impact** – Cet événement unique est important car il correspond à ce que les scientifiques attendaient d’un type de particule de matière noire appelé WIMP (particule massive faiblement interactive). Si cela est confirmé, ce serait la première preuve directe de particules de matière noire, une découverte que les chercheurs cherchent depuis des décennies.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à collecter des données pour voir s’ils peuvent détecter d’autres événements similaires. D’autres expériences dans le monde essaieront aussi de confirmer ou d’infirmer ce résultat. Ce processus aidera à déterminer si cet éclair était vraiment causé par la matière noire ou autre chose.

**Une phrase clé** – Pour la première fois, les scientifiques pourraient avoir aperçu des particules de matière noire grâce à un rare signal d’énergie détecté en profondeur sous terre.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos detectan por primera vez una posible señal de materia oscura
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La materia oscura es una sustancia misteriosa que forma gran parte del universo, pero no se puede ver. Los científicos creen que mantiene unidas a las galaxias, pero nunca han detectado directamente sus partículas.

**Qué pasó** – Entre 2023 y 2024, un experimento llamado LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) en Dakota del Sur registró un raro destello de energía en un tanque con 10 toneladas de xenón líquido. Este destello podría haber sido causado por una partícula de materia oscura que chocó con un átomo de xenón. El equipo de LZ compartió este hallazgo el 1 de septiembre de 2026, tras analizar 220 días de datos.

**Impacto** – Este evento único es importante porque coincide con lo que los científicos esperaban de un tipo de partícula de materia oscura llamada WIMP (partícula masiva débilmente interactiva). Si se confirma, sería la primera evidencia directa de partículas de materia oscura, un descubrimiento que los investigadores han buscado durante décadas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán recopilando más datos para ver si pueden detectar eventos similares. Otros experimentos en el mundo también intentarán confirmar o refutar este resultado. Este proceso ayudará a saber si el destello fue realmente causado por materia oscura o por otra cosa.

**Una frase clave** – Por primera vez, los científicos podrían haber detectado partículas de materia oscura gracias a una rara señal de energía captada bajo tierra.
